title: Talking like a person
goal: Put the twenty units together and add the last layer: the small particles, the swallowed syllables and the ready-made phrases that separate correct Indonesian from natural Indonesian.
bekal: use *sih*, *dong*, *kok*, *deh*, *lho*, *kan* and *nih* without thinking about them
understand everyday speech that drops prefixes and shortens words
hold a whole conversation, open to close, without English

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Terakhir di kantor
dialogs.intro: Sarah's contract is ending. Rina finds her packing up her desk.

notes: **Read that dialogue again and notice what is not there.** No *me-* prefixes. No *sedang*, no *akan*, no *tidak*. Almost every sentence is a bare root with a particle stuck on the end. This is what Indonesian actually sounds like between friends, and you can now understand all of it.

**Beneran, banget, makasih, aja, balik, nih.** These are the spoken forms of *benar*, *sangat*, *terima kasih*, *saja*, *kembali*, *ini*. Learning six words has just unlocked a great deal of real speech.

**Kok appears twice, doing two different jobs.** At the start of a question it means "how come, why": *Kok cepat banget?* At the end of a statement it insists gently: *Saya mau balik lagi, kok* — "I really do want to come back". Same word, opposite ends of the sentence.
**Names get shortened, constantly.** Rina becomes *Rin*, Budi becomes *Bud*, Sarah might well become *Sar*. It is a sign of closeness, not laziness, and being shortened is a small compliment.

**Biasa aja — "it was nothing".** The standard deflection of thanks between friends, alongside *santai aja* ("relax, no problem") and *nggak apa-apa*. *Sama-sama* is the neutral, slightly more formal answer you learned in Unit 1.

grammars.title: The particles
body: These carry no dictionary meaning; they carry attitude. Getting them right is the last ten per cent that makes Indonesian sound like a person rather than a textbook.
after: You do not have to use these. You do have to understand them, because Indonesians use them in almost every sentence. Start with *ya*, *kan* and *dong* — they are the easiest to place and the hardest to get wrong.
⚠️ Do not pile them up. One particle per sentence is normal; three is comic.

grammars.title: Spoken shortcuts, collected
body: The full list of the swaps that will get you from written Indonesian to overheard Indonesian.
after: 💬 And in Jakarta, *saya* and *kamu* often become *gue* and *lo*. Understand them; use them only once you are sure of the company. In writing, especially to anyone senior, keep to *saya* and *Bapak/Ibu*.

blocks.text: *Sudah dulu, ya* — "that's enough for now" — is the standard way to end a conversation or a phone call without seeming abrupt. It is the counterpart of *Apa kabar?* at the other end, and having both means you can open and close like a native.

rows: How do you say it in Indonesian?

blocks.text: One last thing, and it matters more than any table. Indonesians are, as a rule, delighted when a foreigner speaks their language — even badly, even slowly, even wrongly. You will be praised for sentences you know are broken. Take the encouragement, keep going, and say the next sentence.
